claim: Severe alcoholic hepatitis (SAH) is a distinct clinical syndrome that can develop suddenly and quickly lead to liver failure.
source: Severe alcoholic hepatitis (SAH) is a distinct clinical syndrome that can develop suddenly and quickly lead to liver failure.
evidence: This is stated as established medical knowledge in the introduction.

claim: SAH carries a 28-day mortality ranging from 30% to 50%.
source: It carries a particularly poor prognosis with a 28-day mortality ranging from 30% to 50% (Dugum et al., 2015; Thursz and Morgan, 2016; Sehrawat et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published studies.

claim: Massive IgA and IgG deposition occurs in ballooned hepatocytes in SAH livers.
source: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining by using anti-human immunoglobulin (Ig) antibodies demonstrated massive IgA and IgG deposition in ballooned hepatocytes in SAH livers, while none of the hepatocytes were stained with anti-human Ig antibodies in liver tissue sections from healthy donors (HD) except for positive staining in some hepatic sinusoid cells (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The levels of IgA and IgG were dramatically increased in all SAH livers compared with donor livers.
source: Western blot analysis demonstrated that the levels of IgA and IgG were dramatically increased in all SAH livers as compared with the donor livers (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot analysis data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: IgM levels were significantly increased in SAH livers.
source: The IgM but not the IgE level was also significantly increased in SAH livers.
evidence: This is stated based on Western blot analysis results.

claim: IgA and IgG isotypes were major immunoglobulins in SAH livers.
source: IgA and IgG isotypes were major Ig in SAH livers (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: IgG1 was the predominant IgG subclass in SAH livers.
source: Further analysis of IgG subclasses demonstrated that the IgG subclass levels – predominantly IgG1 – were significantly higher in SAH livers than that in HD (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: On average approximately 40% of hepatocytes (ranging from 4% to 80%) were IgG positive in SAH livers.
source: In contrast, on average ~40% of the hepatocytes (ranging from 4% to 80%) were IgG positive in the SAH livers (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of IHC staining using HALO Image Analysis Software on 45 SAH livers.

claim: Few IgG+ hepatocytes were identified in donor livers.
source: Few IgG+ hepatocytes were identified in donor livers.
evidence: This is stated based on quantitative analysis of IHC staining.

claim: Both C3d and C4d complement fragments are present in ballooning hepatocytes in SAH livers but not in donor livers.
source: IHC staining showed the presence of both C3d and C4d in ballooning hepatocytes in SAH livers but not in the donor livers (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC staining data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: IgG co-stained with C3d and C4d in ballooning hepatocytes.
source: Double staining for IgG and complement fragments C3d or C4d showed IgG co-stained with C3d or C4d in ballooning hepatocytes (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by double staining data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: IgG deposition in hepatocytes was associated with activation of complement.
source: These results indicated that IgG deposition in hepatocytes was associated with activation of complement.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization of IgG with complement fragments C3d and C4d.

claim: Complement activation including the presence of C3d and C4d in SAH liver was confirmed by western blot analysis.
source: Furthermore, complement activation including the presence of C3d and C4d in SAH liver was confirmed by western blot analysis (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Ig extracted from SAH livers exhibited hepatocyte killing efficacy in an antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) assay.
source: However, the hepatocyte killing efficacy was significantly increased when the same levels of Ig extracted from SAH livers were added into the hepatocytes/PBMCs co-culture system (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ADCC assay data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Serum Ig from SAH patients did not increase hepatocyte killing compared to isotype control.
source: Compared to isotype control human Ig from HD, no increased hepatocyte killing was observed when peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) (effector cells) from HD were added into cultured human hepatocytes (target cells) in the presence of serum Ig from SAH patients.
evidence: This is stated based on ADCC assay results.

claim: Both IgG and IgA are present in hepatic sinusoid endothelial cells but not hepatocytes in donor livers.
source: Images of confocal microscopy showed the presence of both IgG and IgA in hepatic sinusoid endothelial cells but not hepatocytes in the donor livers, while the majority of ballooned hepatocytes co-stained with IgG and IgA in SAH livers (new Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The majority of ballooned hepatocytes co-stained with IgG and IgA in SAH livers.
source: Images of confocal microscopy showed the presence of both IgG and IgA in hepatic sinusoid endothelial cells but not hepatocytes in the donor livers, while the majority of ballooned hepatocytes co-stained with IgG and IgA in SAH livers (new Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Heavy IgG and IgA deposition occurs on hepatocyte membrane in SAH livers.
source: Further, co-staining with β-catenin detected heavy IgG and IgA deposition on hepatocyte membrane (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-staining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: IgG and IgA on hepatocyte membrane were co-stained with C4d.
source: Interestingly, the IgG and IgA on hepatocyte membrane were co-stained with C4d as well (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by triple staining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 346 autoantigens were shared by IgG antibodies in all five SAH livers.
source: The total numbers of the shared autoantigens recognized by the IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgE isotypes were 346, 319, 194, and 10 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), respectively, suggesting that the shared autoantibodies of the IgG and IgA isotypes were the most prevalent, while the counterparts of IgE isotype were the scarcest.
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 319 autoantigens were shared by IgA antibodies in all five SAH livers.
source: The total numbers of the shared autoantigens recognized by the IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgE isotypes were 346, 319, 194, and 10 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), respectively, suggesting that the shared autoantibodies of the IgG and IgA isotypes were the most prevalent, while the counterparts of IgE isotype were the scarcest.
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 194 autoantigens were shared by IgM antibodies in all five SAH livers.
source: The total numbers of the shared autoantigens recognized by the IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgE isotypes were 346, 319, 194, and 10 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), respectively, suggesting that the shared autoantibodies of the IgG and IgA isotypes were the most prevalent, while the counterparts of IgE isotype were the scarcest.
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 10 autoantigens were shared by IgE antibodies in all five SAH livers.
source: The total numbers of the shared autoantigens recognized by the IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgE isotypes were 346, 319, 194, and 10 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), respectively, suggesting that the shared autoantibodies of the IgG and IgA isotypes were the most prevalent, while the counterparts of IgE isotype were the scarcest.
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 95 shared IgG autoantigens were identified by donor liver samples.
source: Although 95 shared IgG autoantigens were identified by the donor liver samples, 79 (83.2%) of them were also shared by the SAH livers (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 79 (83.2%) of the 95 shared IgG autoantigens from donor livers were also shared by SAH livers.
source: Although 95 shared IgG autoantigens were identified by the donor liver samples, 79 (83.2%) of them were also shared by the SAH livers (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 267 SAH-shared autoantigens were not found in donor livers.
source: More importantly, a large fraction (i.e., 267 proteins) of the SAH-shared autoantigens were not found in the donor livers (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 45 autoantigens were commonly recognized by IgG isotype autoantibodies in liver tissue extracted from different liver diseases.
source: By Venn diagram analysis 45, 41, 68, and 8 autoantigens were commonly recognized by IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgE isotype autoantibodies in liver tissue extracted from different liver diseases (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: 188 unique IgG autoantigens were recognized by tissue homogenates from SAH livers.
source: 188 unique IgG autoantigens, 45 unique IgA autoantigens, and 7 unique IgM autoantigens were recognized by tissue homogenates from the SAH livers, whereas the second highest in this category was HBV livers in which 1 unique IgG autoantigen, 88 unique IgA autoantigens, and 25 unique IgM autoantigens were identified (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: 435 shared bacterial antigens were recognized by IgG antibodies in the five SAH livers.
source: For instance, only one bacterial antigen was commonly recognized by IgG antibodies from HD livers, but 435 shared bacterial antigens (about 10.2% of 4256 purified E. coli proteins) were recognized by IgG antibodies in the five SAH livers (Figure 4F), and 466 shared bacterial antigens were recognized by IgG antibodies in the five AC livers (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by E. coli proteome array data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Only one bacterial antigen was commonly recognized by IgG antibodies from healthy donor livers.
source: For instance, only one bacterial antigen was commonly recognized by IgG antibodies from HD livers, but 435 shared bacterial antigens (about 10.2% of 4256 purified E. coli proteins) were recognized by IgG antibodies in the five SAH livers (Figure 4F), and 466 shared bacterial antigens were recognized by IgG antibodies in the five AC livers (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by E. coli proteome array data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: 466 shared bacterial antigens were recognized by IgG antibodies in the five AC livers.
source: For instance, only one bacterial antigen was commonly recognized by IgG antibodies from HD livers, but 435 shared bacterial antigens (about 10.2% of 4256 purified E. coli proteins) were recognized by IgG antibodies in the five SAH livers (Figure 4F), and 466 shared bacterial antigens were recognized by IgG antibodies in the five AC livers (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by E. coli proteome array data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Unique IgG or IgA bacterial antigens were only identified by using liver tissue from SAH or AC.
source: Unique IgG or IgA bacterial antigens were only identified by using liver tissue from SAH or AC (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: 694 human proteins were reproducibly identified by E. coli protein-captured IgG antibodies from the five SAH livers.
source: At a stringent cutoff value (e.g., SD=10) 694, 796, 451, and 42 human proteins were reproducibly identified by E. coli protein-captured IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgE antibodies from the five SAH livers, respectively (Figure 5C and antibody-recognized protein sets in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by HuProt array data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 796 human proteins were reproducibly identified by E. coli protein-captured IgA antibodies from the five SAH livers.
source: At a stringent cutoff value (e.g., SD=10) 694, 796, 451, and 42 human proteins were reproducibly identified by E. coli protein-captured IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgE antibodies from the five SAH livers, respectively (Figure 5C and antibody-recognized protein sets in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by HuProt array data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 74.06% of E. coli binding IgG recognized proteins were also found to be autoantigens recognized by Ig recovered directly from the five SAH livers.
source: Strikingly, many of these E. coli binding Ig recognized proteins (74.06%, 76.46%, 48.39%, and 49.41%, respectively) were also found to be the autoantigens recognized by Ig recovered directly from the five SAH livers.
evidence: This is stated based on comparison of E. coli-captured Ig and directly extracted Ig data.

claim: Proteins recognized by IgG antibodies from SAH livers were significantly over-represented in eight cellular components including cytosol, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondrion, focal adhesion extracellular exosome, mitochondrial intermembrane space, and ruffle membrane.
source: Proteins recognized by IgG antibodies from SAH livers were significantly over-represented in eight cellular components including cytosol, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondrion, focal adhesion extracellular exosome, mitochondrial intermembrane space, and ruffle membrane, while autoantigens recognized by IgA antibodies from SAH livers were over-represented in cytosol and cytoplasm (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Autoantigens recognized by IgA antibodies from SAH livers were over-represented in cytosol and cytoplasm.
source: Proteins recognized by IgG antibodies from SAH livers were significantly over-represented in eight cellular components including cytosol, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondrion, focal adhesion extracellular exosome, mitochondrial intermembrane space, and ruffle membrane, while autoantigens recognized by IgA antibodies from SAH livers were over-represented in cytosol and cytoplasm (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: E. coli-captured IgG and IgA from SAH livers recognized five out of eight cellular components which were recognized by Ig directly extracted from SAH livers.
source: Interestingly, E. coli-captured IgG and IgA from SAH livers recognized five out of eight cellular components which were recognized by Ig directly extracted from SAH livers (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: This overlap of cellular components recognized by E. coli-captured and directly extracted Ig was observed only in SAH livers.
source: This was observed only in SAH livers (Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated based on comparison across different liver diseases.

claim: Both LPS and LTA were present in liver tissue from SAH patients compared to controls, especially in the inflammatory areas.
source: Both LPS and LTA were in liver tissue from SAH patients cf. controls (Figure 7A), especially in the inflammatory areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC staining data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The increase of LPS levels in SAH liver tissues was confirmed by using Pierce Chromogenic Endotoxin Quant Kit.
source: The increase of LPS levels in SAH liver tissues was confirmed by using Pierce Chromogenic Endotoxin Quant Kit (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative LPS measurement shown in Figure 7B.

claim: CD20+ and CD138+ cells were localized in the inflammatory areas of SAH livers, with none in HD livers.
source: IHC staining for CD20+ and CD138+ cells revealed that most of these cells were localized in the inflammatory areas of SAH livers, with none in HD livers (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC staining data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: 87 genes representing immunoglobulin fragments showed robust and stable expression in SAH livers but not in HD livers.
source: Interestingly, 87 identified genes representing Ig fragments showed a robust and stable expression in SAH livers but not in HD livers (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Deposition of Ig antibodies may contribute to hepatocyte ballooning degeneration and necrotic damage in SAH.
source: Therefore, deposition of Ig antibodies may contribute to the hepatocyte ballooning degeneration and necrotic damage in SAH.
evidence: This is inferred from the hepatocyte killing efficacy data and complement activation findings.

claim: Antibody deposition with complement activation and immune cell activation may result in acute liver failure due to antibody-mediated inflammation.
source: Antibody deposition, with complement activation as well as immune cell activation, may result in acute liver failure due to antibody-mediated inflammation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings presented in the study.

claim: Anti-bacterial antibodies and/or plasma cells originating from gut translocate to the liver due to gut leakiness caused by excessive alcohol drinking.
source: Our data support the hypothesis that anti-bacterial antibodies and/or plasma cells originating from gut translocate to the liver due to gut leakiness caused by excessive alcohol drinking and that these hepatic plasma cells produce antibodies which not only recognize intestinal bacterial antigens but also cross-react with antigens of human hepatocytes (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Hepatic plasma cells produce antibodies which not only recognize intestinal bacterial antigens but also cross-react with antigens of human hepatocytes.
source: Our data support the hypothesis that anti-bacterial antibodies and/or plasma cells originating from gut translocate to the liver due to gut leakiness caused by excessive alcohol drinking and that these hepatic plasma cells produce antibodies which not only recognize intestinal bacterial antigens but also cross-react with antigens of human hepatocytes (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: Leaky gut is a digestive condition in which bacteria and toxins are able to pass from the gastrointestinal tract to extraintestinal sites.
source: Leaky gut, also known as increased intestinal permeability, is a digestive condition in which bacteria and toxins are able to pass from the gastrointestinal tract to extraintestinal sites and facilitate an increased ingress of inflammatory cytokines and endotoxin to the liver (Bajaj, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: No antibody-mediated rejection was observed in SAH patients following liver transplantation.
source: Importantly, no antibody-mediated rejection was observed in SAH patients following liver transplantation (Weeks et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Serum from SAH patients did not show hepatocyte killing efficacy in vitro.
source: Unlike antibody-mediated autoimmune disease where systemic B cells produce autoantibodies against self-antigens and unlike the fact that autoimmune diseases can be transferred from an affected patient to a normal individual by the transfer of patient-derived serum (or Ig), serum from SAH patients did not show hepatocyte killing efficacy in vitro.
evidence: This is stated based on ADCC assay results.

claim: Gut-derived plasma cells are resident in SAH livers and produce anti-bacteria antibodies which strongly cross-react with hepatocyte antigens.
source: It is perhaps more likely that gut-derived plasma cells were resident in SAH livers, and these plasma cells produce anti-bacteria antibodies which strongly cross-react with hepatocyte antigens.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The diseased liver absorbs gut-derived and locally produced antibodies without releasing them to the circulation.
source: The diseased liver absorbs these gut-derived and locally produced antibodies without releasing them to the circulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that liver Ig but not serum Ig showed hepatocyte killing efficacy.

claim: Activation of complement through the classical pathway leads to ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes which is the predominant mode of injury in alcoholic hepatitis.
source: With the functional deposition of antibodies in the SAH liver (Figure 2), activation of complement through the classical pathway which has been reported previously (Shen et al., 2014) leads to ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes which is the predominant mode of injury in alcoholic hepatitis and untreatable inflammation.
evidence: This is stated based on the findings and a citation to previous work.

claim: The new transplanted liver will not be damaged because the pathogenesis involving the consequences of leaky gut pathology will end quickly as long as the recipient remains abstinent.
source: Therefore, it is reassuring that the new transplanted liver will not be damaged because the pathogenesis, involving the consequences of leaky gut pathology, will end quickly as long as the recipient remains abstinent, by which the new liver is not threatened by the SAH process.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: Studies have established connections between alcohol abuse, disruption of gut microbial homeostasis, and alcoholic liver disease.
source: Studies have established connections between alcohol abuse, disruption of gut microbial homeostasis, and alcoholic liver disease (ALD).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: It has been speculated for over four decades that antibodies targeting intestinal microbes might play a role in pathogenesis of ALD.
source: It has been speculated for over four decades that antibodies targeting intestinal microbes might play a role in pathogenesis of ALD (Bjorneboe et al., 1972; Simjee et al., 1975; Kanagasundaram et al., 1977; Kater et al., 1979; Trevisan et al., 1983; Koskinas et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated with citations to historical studies.

claim: The presence of IgA and IgG on the cell membrane of hepatocytes was detected by direct immunofluorescence in patients with ALD.
source: For example, the presence of IgA and IgG on the cell membrane of hepatocytes was detected by direct immunofluorescence in patients with ALD, and the percentage of IgG-positive hepatocytes correlated with transaminase levels, independently of the histological findings (Trevisan et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The percentage of IgG-positive hepatocytes correlated with transaminase levels, independently of the histological findings.
source: For example, the presence of IgA and IgG on the cell membrane of hepatocytes was detected by direct immunofluorescence in patients with ALD, and the percentage of IgG-positive hepatocytes correlated with transaminase levels, independently of the histological findings (Trevisan et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Human livers contain IgA-secreting cells originating from Peyer's patches and directed against intestinal antigens.
source: A recent study (Moro-Sibilot et al., 2016) confirmed that human livers contained IgA-secreting cells originating from Peyer's patches and directed against intestinal antigens.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Livers from mice with ethanol-induced injury contain increased numbers of IgA-secreting cells and have IgA deposits in sinusoids.
source: Interestingly, livers from mice with ethanol-induced injury contain increased numbers of IgA-secreting cells and have IgA deposits in sinusoids (Moro-Sibilot et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: SAH liver tissue sections showed histologic features including macrovesicular steatosis, neutrophilic lobular inflammation, ballooning hepatocyte degeneration, Mallory-Denk bodies, and portal and pericellular fibrosis.
source: Liver tissue sections with H&E staining from SAH patients showed histologic features of SAH including macrovesicular steatosis, neutrophilic lobular inflammation, ballooning hepatocyte degeneration, Mallory-Denk bodies, and portal and pericellular fibrosis (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: IgG plays a critical role in the classical complement activation pathway.
source: IgG, especially IgG1, plays a critical role in the classical complement activation pathway.
evidence: This is stated as established immunological knowledge.

claim: Increased gut bacterial antigens in the SAH liver are associated with increased B cells and plasma cells.
source: These results suggest that increased gut bacterial antigens in the SAH liver are associated with increased B cells and plasma cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization of bacterial antigens with B and plasma cells.

claim: Infiltrating B and plasma cells secrete Ig that not only have anti-intestinal antigen activity but also cross-react with hepatocyte antigens.
source: These results suggest that infiltrating B and plasma cells secrete Ig that not only have anti-intestinal antigen activity but also cross-react with hepatocyte antigens.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing Ig gene expression and the proteome array data showing cross-reactivity.

claim: Ig antibodies deposited in hepatocytes might not be produced systemically but by plasma cells infiltrating the liver.
source: Based on our findings that Ig extracted from SAH livers but not present in the serum exhibited hepatocyte killing efficacy (Figure 2G), we suspected that Ig antibodies deposited in hepatocytes might not be produced systemically but by plasma cells infiltrating the liver.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential hepatocyte killing efficacy of liver Ig versus serum Ig.

claim: Antibodies secreted into the gut mostly target bacteria and bacterial products.
source: Antibodies secreted into the gut mostly target bacteria and bacterial products (Kato et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: There exist a large number of cross-reacting antibodies that recognize both bacterial and human proteins in the SAH livers.
source: These results demonstrated that there exist a large number of cross-reacting antibodies that recognize both bacterial and human proteins in the SAH livers.
evidence: This is concluded from the E. coli-captured Ig data showing recognition of human proteins.

claim: Antibodies reacting against the mitochondrial human pyruvate dehydrogenase complex which are the serologic hallmark of PBC cross-react with the E. coli pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
source: Antibodies reacting against the mitochondrial human pyruvate dehydrogenase complex which are the serologic hallmark of PBC cross-react with the E. coli pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, implicating E. coli infection in the pathogenesis of PBC (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Patients with PBC had a much higher number of inducible IgM-producing B cells in peripheral blood and each B cell produced a greater quantity of IgM protein compared with control.
source: Interestingly, patients with PBC had a much higher number of inducible IgM-producing B cells in peripheral blood and each B cell produced a greater quantity of IgM protein compared with control (Kikuchi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: A strong association between increasing serum IgA level and disease progressing in patients with chronic HBV infection has been reported.
source: A strong association between increasing serum IgA level and disease progressing in patients with chronic HBV infection has been reported (Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Serum IgG was increased in patients with chronic hepatitis C with respect to both alcoholics and healthy controls.
source: Similarly, serum IgG was increased in patients with chronic hepatitis C with respect to both alcoholics and healthy controls (Gonzàlez-Quintela et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Alcohol-induced changes of gut microbiota composition may contribute to the development of anti-bacterial antibodies that cross-reacted with human antigens.
source: The differing gut microbiota between actively drinking patients with cirrhosis and those with alcoholic hepatitis (Llopis et al., 2016; Llorente et al., 2017; Duan et al., 2019) supports the notion that alcohol-induced changes of gut microbiota composition may contribute to the development of anti-bacterial antibodies that cross-reacted with human antigens.
evidence: This is inferred from cited studies showing differences in gut microbiota.

claim: SAH is an acute-on-chronic liver failure.
source: SAH is an acute-on-chronic liver failure.
evidence: This is stated as established medical knowledge.

claim: Cross-reacting anti-bacterial autoantibodies translocated to the liver may determine the progress from chronic liver disease toward acute hepatitis.
source: Cross-reacting anti-bacterial autoantibodies translocated to the liver may determine the progress from chronic liver disease toward acute hepatitis.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings.

claim: Preventing gut leakiness caused by alcohol drinking may prevent SAH.
source: First, preventing gut leakiness caused by alcohol drinking may prevent SAH.
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic strategy based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: Eliminating antibody-producing B/plasma cells in the liver by using anti-CD20 may serve as a therapeutic strategy.
source: Second, eliminating antibody-producing B/plasma cells in the liver by using anti-CD20 may serve.
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic strategy based on the findings.

claim: A trial using complement inhibitors such as eculizumab may be worth considering.
source: Finally, a trial using complement inhibitors such as eculizumab may be worth considering.
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic strategy based on the findings of complement activation.
